name: Bhadrapur
blurb: A Terai town in Jhapa whose airport, often listed as Chandragadhi, is the air gateway to Kanchenjunga and the Ilam tea hills. Flights from Kathmandu take about 45 minutes and the drive to Taplejung starts here.
tip: Withdraw cash here or in nearby Birtamod; machines further north are few and often empty.

name: Ilam
blurb: A hill town surrounded by tea gardens on the road between the plains and Taplejung. It is the usual overnight stop on the drive to and from the Kanchenjunga trailheads.

name: Taplejung
blurb: The district headquarters, also called Phungling, and the last proper town before Kanchenjunga. Jeeps for Sekathum leave from its bazaar, and it has the final banks, pharmacies and general shops.
tip: Buy snacks, batteries and any missing basics here; choice shrinks to almost nothing up the valley.

name: Suketar
blurb: The airstrip on the ridge above Taplejung and once the standard start of the Kanchenjunga trek. Scheduled flights are infrequent and often cancelled, so most trekkers now arrive by road.

name: Sekathum
blurb: A few lodges where the Ghunsa Khola meets the Tamor, and for now the usual end of the jeep track from Taplejung. The walk up the Ghunsa gorge begins here. Its height is quoted between 1,575 and 1,670 m.

name: Amjilosa
blurb: A handful of houses and simple lodges on a steep shelf high above the Ghunsa Khola, reached by a hard climb from the river. Its altitude is quoted anywhere between 2,310 and 2,510 m.

name: Gyabla
blurb: A small Sherpa settlement in a forest clearing above the Ghunsa Khola, also written Kyapra. Its lodges break the climb from the gorge to Ghunsa into manageable days.

name: Phale
blurb: A settlement founded by Tibetan refugees on the trail below Ghunsa, with a small monastery and households that weave carpets. It also serves as the winter village for families from Ghunsa.

name: Ghunsa
blurb: The main village of the upper valley: timber houses, a monastery, a police post and the best-stocked lodges on the route. Published heights range from about 3,415 to 3,595 m. The pass route to the south side starts here.
tip: Spend two nights on the way up. It is the last place with a real choice of food and a chance to dry clothes.

name: Kambachen
blurb: A summer yak-herding settlement of stone houses and a few lodges on a grassy flat, with the north face of Jannu at the head of the side valley. A sensible second acclimatization stop before Lhonak.

name: Lhonak
blurb: Basic stone lodges on a cold, sandy plain beside the Kanchenjunga Glacier, and the last place most people sleep before the north base camp. Expect wind, hard frost and very simple food.
tip: If you sleep badly or wake with a headache here, skip Pangpema and go down to Kambachen.

name: Pangpema
blurb: The north base camp of Kanchenjunga: a grassy shelf with a stone hut above the glacier, facing the mountain's north face. Most trekkers visit on a day walk from Lhonak rather than sleep here.

name: Sele La
blurb: A saddle on the ridge route between Ghunsa and Cheram, with simple huts close by where trekkers sleep before the higher passes. It is usually given as 4,290 m, though 4,170 and 4,480 m also appear in print.

name: Sinion La
blurb: The first pass south of the Sele La huts, a rocky notch at about 4,440 m reached by a rough rising traverse. A few sources put it nearer 4,650 m.

name: Mirgin La
blurb: The middle pass of the Ghunsa to Cheram traverse at about 4,480 m, marked by prayer flags, with Jannu close by in clear weather. Fresh snow makes the trail on either side hard to find.

name: Sinelapche La
blurb: The last and highest crossing of the traverse, usually given as 4,646 m, before a steep descent of nearly 800 m to Cheram. Higher figures, up to about 4,840 m, appear on some itineraries.

name: Cheram
blurb: A cluster of lodges in the Simbuwa Khola valley, also spelled Tseram, where the pass route from Ghunsa meets the trail to the south base camp. Forest starts again just below it.

name: Ramche
blurb: A wide meadow with a small lake and a couple of basic lodges beside the Yalung Glacier, the last place to sleep on the south side. Blue sheep often graze the slopes above.

name: Oktang
blurb: A chorten hung with prayer flags on the moraine beside the Yalung Glacier, at about 4,730 m. It is as far as trekkers go on the south side and looks up the glacier to Kanchenjunga's south-west face.

name: Tortong
blurb: Two or three lodges in tall conifer and rhododendron forest beside the Simbuwa Khola. It splits the long descent from Cheram to Yamphudin.

name: Lasiya Bhanjyang
blurb: The forested ridge crossing between the Simbuwa Khola and Yamphudin, also called Lamite Bhanjyang and listed at 3,310 to 3,415 m. A very large landslide scars the slope beside the trail.

name: Yamphudin
blurb: A spread-out farming village of Limbu, Rai, Sherpa and Gurung families at the foot of the south-side trail, with a conservation area checkpoint. A jeep track reaches it when conditions allow.

name: Olangchung Gola
blurb: A trading village of the Walung people on an old route to Tibet, about two days up the Tamor from the Kanchenjunga trail. Its monastery and wooden houses see very few trekkers.

name: Tumlingtar
blurb: A small town on a river terrace above the Arun with the airstrip for the Makalu trek. Jeeps for Khandbari and Num wait outside the terminal. Its altitude is listed between about 400 and 520 m.

name: Khandbari
blurb: The district headquarters of Sankhuwasabha, on the ridge above Tumlingtar. It is the last place with banks, cash machines and a full bazaar before the Makalu trail.

name: Num
blurb: A ridge-top village at the end of the jeep road, facing Seduwa across the deep Arun gorge. The Makalu trek starts with the long descent to the river from here.

name: Seduwa
blurb: A farming village of Rai and Sherpa families above the west bank of the Arun, and the entry point to Makalu Barun National Park, where permits are registered.

name: Tashigaon
blurb: The last permanent village on the Makalu trail, a Sherpa settlement among millet terraces at the foot of the Khongma ridge. Beyond it there are only seasonal lodges.
tip: Top up on snacks and ask the lodge owners which huts higher up are open.

name: Khongma Danda
blurb: A few lodges on a narrow forested ridge at about 3,500 m, the first stop above the villages and the place to acclimatize before the passes. Water is limited, especially in spring.

name: Shipton La
blurb: The highest of the passes between Khongma and the Barun valley, quoted at anything from 4,125 to 4,229 m and named after the British explorer Eric Shipton. It holds snow late into spring.

name: Keke La
blurb: The second main pass on the way to the Barun valley, at roughly 4,150 m, reached after the small lake of Kalo Pokhari. The descent beyond it leads to the lodges at Dobate.

name: Dobate
blurb: A pair of lodges on a forested shelf below the Keke La, also written Dobato, and the staging point for the drop into the Barun valley. Published heights run from about 3,550 to 3,860 m.

name: Yangle Kharka
blurb: A broad meadow on the floor of the Barun valley with a few lodges, enclosed by rock walls streaked with waterfalls. It is the first flat, open ground after the landslide section.

name: Langmale Kharka
blurb: A yak pasture with stone lodges at about 4,410 m, the last stop before base camp and a common place for an extra acclimatization night.

name: Shershong
blurb: A stony flat at about 4,630 m where the upper Barun valley bends and the south face of Makalu comes into full view. Herders and camping groups use it.

name: Makalu Base Camp
blurb: Stone lodges on gravel flats beside the Barun river at about 4,870 m, below the south face of Makalu. Climbers use a higher camp further up the glacier; for trekkers this is the end of the trail.
